recent_posts.title: cuTile.jl 0.3: CUDA.jl integration, and even better performance & latency
recent_posts.summary: cuTile.jl v0.3 brings major improvements to GPU tile kernel programming in Julia. Key highlights include first-class CUDA.jl integration via the @cuda backend=cuTile macro, performance that now matches or exceeds cuTile Python on all benchmarks (with notable wins like +63% on FMHA attention and +37% on Layer Norm forward), dramatically reduced time-to-first-launch comparable to standard CUDA.jl kernels, new array slicing support via view/@view for TileArrays, and a tile-vectorized Philox2x32-7 RNG with both in-kernel and host-side APIs covering all major numeric types.

recent_posts.title: TestItems – Modern Julia testing
recent_posts.summary: TestItems is a modern testing framework for Julia that supports parallel testing, test isolation, setup steps, and test filtering. It integrates with VSCode and can be used with Revise for automatic test reruns, or with AI agents via julia-mcp. The post serves as a written companion to a video tutorial aimed at Julia package developers.

recent_posts.title: cuTile.jl 0.2: New features, improved performance, and Julia 1.13 support
recent_posts.summary: cuTile.jl v0.2 is a major update to the Julia package for writing GPU kernels using NVIDIA's tile-based programming model. Key additions include native `for` loop support (replacing a `while`-loop workaround), a new `ct.@fpmode` macro for scoped floating-point mode control, keyword arguments for most operations, experimental host-level abstractions (`ct.Tiled`) for broadcasting and reductions without explicit kernel code, and in-kernel `print`/`println` debugging. New atomic operations (`atomic_max`, `atomic_min`, `atomic_or`, etc.) and Julia 1.13 support are also included. Under the hood, a new multi-pass optimization pipeline with algebraic simplification, comparison strength reduction, LICM, constant folding, and alias-aware token ordering dramatically improves generated Tile IR quality — reducing a layernorm kernel from 10,036 to 3,253 SASS instructions. All ported examples now perform within 10% of their cuTile Python counterparts.

recent_posts.title: Ray Tracing in Makie: From Research Data to Photorealistic Renders
recent_posts.summary: RayMakie and Hikari are newly announced packages that bring physically-based GPU ray tracing to the Makie visualization ecosystem in Julia, enabling photorealistic rendering of scientific data directly within Julia workflows.

recent_posts.title: What Agentic AI “Vibe Coding” In The Hands Of Actual Programmers / Engineers
recent_posts.summary: Effective AI-assisted coding requires deep domain knowledge and precise prompting. The author demonstrates how experienced programmers use LLMs like Claude by providing detailed context, pointing to specific code locations, showing examples, and explaining architectural patterns—treating the AI like a grad student who needs thorough guidance. Two complex refactoring examples show prompts that include exact file paths, existing implementations, test locations, and clear explanations of why changes are needed, contrasting sharply with vague "solve this for me" requests from inexperienced users.

recent_posts.title: Julia GPU ODE solvers outperform JAX and PyTorch by 20x to 100x
recent_posts.summary: Julia's GPU-accelerated ODE (ordinary differential equation) solvers achieve 20x-100x performance improvements over JAX and PyTorch due to fundamental architectural differences in how they utilize GPUs. The performance gap stems from Julia's approach to GPU acceleration versus the standard machine learning library approach. The DiffEqGPU library now supports multi-GPU parallelism, enabling automated distribution across multiple CUDA devices for scientific computing workloads.

recent_posts.title: Introducing SciML Health Bots: Lowering Barriers While Raising Standards
recent_posts.summary: SciML introduces Health Bots, an automated system designed to improve package maintenance standards while making it easier for contributors to participate in the ecosystem. The initiative aims to balance accessibility for new contributors with maintaining high quality standards across SciML packages.

recent_posts.title: How to Integrate Julia Code Within a Python Program
recent_posts.summary: juliacall enables Python developers to call Julia code directly from Python programs, combining Python's ecosystem with Julia's performance. The tutorial covers installation via pip, basic usage examples, and a complete walkthrough of integrating a custom Julia package (using OrdinaryDiffEq.jl for simulations) into a Python project. Key steps include setting up the Julia package structure, configuring juliapkg.json to locate Julia dependencies, and calling Julia functions from Python while converting results back to NumPy arrays for further processing.

recent_posts.title: Launching the Julia Security Working Group
recent_posts.summary: The Julia programming language community announces the formation of a Security Working Group. This initiative aims to strengthen security practices and vulnerability management within the Julia ecosystem, providing a dedicated team to handle security concerns for the language and its packages.

recent_posts.title: Simplifying Julia Package Integration with Extensions
recent_posts.summary: Package extensions in Julia allow conditional code loading based on user dependencies, avoiding unnecessary load times for unused functionality. The mechanism uses weak dependencies and extension modules in an `ext` directory that automatically activate when both the base package and trigger package are loaded. A practical example demonstrates extending an Averages.jl package with DataFrame support through the AveragesDataFramesExt extension, requiring updates to Project.toml with `[weakdeps]` and `[extensions]` sections. This pattern enables better composability while maintaining lean core packages.

top_posts.title: Diagramming + Data Visualization with Julia
top_posts.summary: Vizagrams.jl is a Julia package that blends diagramming and data visualization. It offers a diagramming Domain Specific Language (DSL) with a data visualization grammar built on top of it, inspired by the Haskell library Diagrams. The package allows for creating complex visualizations by combining primitive graphical objects and applying stylistic and geometric transformations. It supports the creation of visualizations similar to those produced by Vega-Lite and can be integrated into notebooks like Jupyter or Pluto for interactive experimentation.
